## Refined Questions and Analysis Choices

# Central Question:
What is the relationship between temporal / land cover factors and fast fire
events (high mean growth rate per event)?

#Supporting Questions:
What is the relationship between temporal /land cover factors and the
longest fire events (duration)?
Is there a relationship between land cover and maximum, mean, minimum daily fire
growth per event?

# Observations and Variables

There are a total of 4329 observations (fire events) available to use

Variable: ig_month Description: The month of the earliest date contained
in the event

Variable: ig_year Description: The year of the earliest date contained
in the event.

Variable: event_dur Description: Duration of the event in days

Variable: mx_grw_km2 Description: Maximum daily fire growth per event in
square kilometers

Variable: mn_grw_km2 Description: Minimum daily fire growth per event in
square kilometers

Variable: mu_grw_km2 Description: Mean daily fire growth per event in
square kilometers

Variable: lc_name Description: Character string of the landcover type
from the year before the fire.

# Intended Comparison / Unresolved Data Limitations

An intended comparison is the central question and first supporting
question. Addressing whether the temporal / land factors are
contributing more to the mean growth rate of the fire events or the duration
of the fire event.

There are no unresolved data limitations, since there are no gaps for
the intended variables.

## What is the relationship between time of year and which land cover types see the fastest fires?

### Response variable: mean growth; Predictors: land cover, month, year

```{r - time of year, land cover type, mean growth two-way ANOVA}
# Group data
mean_growth_group <- california_events_processed %>%
  group_by(lc_name, ig_month, ig_year) %>%
  summarise(mean_growth_rate = mean(mu_grw_km2))

#viewing the grouped data frame and commenting it out after
#view(mean_growth_group)

# create new data frame of just question variables
mean_growth <- california_events_processed %>%
  select(lc_name, ig_month, ig_year, mu_grw_km2)

#viewing the data frame of variables and commenting it out after
#view(mean_growth)

# Format as aov
mean_growth_aov2 <- aov(data = mean_growth, mu_grw_km2 ~ ig_month + lc_name)
summary(mean_growth_aov2)

# Format as lm
mean_growth_anova_2way2 <- lm(data = mean_growth, mu_grw_km2 ~ ig_month + lc_name)
summary(mean_growth_anova_2way2)

# Run a post-hoc test for pairwise differences
TukeyHSD(mean_growth_aov2)

```

mean_growth_anova_plot_separate

###Analysis

To begin to understand if there is a relationship between time of year
and which land cover types experience the fastest fires, we completed a
two way ANOVA as well as Tukey's Honest Significant Differences. We also
created two scatterplots to visualize these relationships, one with all
land cover classes combined and one with them separated. The two way
ANOVA indicated significance for the following land cover classes:
Closed Shrublands (0.000000000247), Evergreen Needleleaf Forests
(0.0000053), Grasslands (0.0000163), Open Shrublands (0.0000000128),
Woody Savannas (0.000894), Savannas (0.002197), and Evergreen Broadleaf
Forests (0.045657), as well as the following months: August (0.001385),
July (0.031237), and October (0.019439). These results can also visually
be seen seen in the scatterplots.

## What is the relationship between time of year and which land cover type sees the longest fast fires?

### Response variable: event length. Predictors: land cover, month, year.

```{r - setting up data frame}
# Group data
event_length_group <- california_events_processed %>%
  group_by(lc_name, ig_month, ig_year) %>%
  summarise(mean_event_dur = mean(event_dur),
            max_event_dur = max(event_dur),
            min_event_dur = min(event_dur)) %>%
  ungroup()

# create new data frame of just question variables
event_length <- california_events_processed %>%
  select(lc_name, ig_month, ig_year, event_dur)

```

Two-way ANOVA

```{r - 2way anova event duration}
# Format as aov
eventlength_aov <- aov(data = event_length, event_dur ~ ig_month + lc_name)
summary(eventlength_aov) # The null hypothesis is that there is no difference in time of year or land cover type in their relationship to fast fire event length. P-values <.05 mean that the null hypothesis can be rejected and that there is a difference between at least two months and at least two land cover types. 

# Run a post-hoc test to look for pairwise differences
TukeyHSD(eventlength_aov)
# There is a significant difference in fast fire event length between september and january (january is higher, p=0.0000328). There is a significant difference in fast fire event length between March and February (February is higher, p= 0.0439883). There is a significant difference in fast fire event length between September and February (February is higher, p= 0.0000000). Other months between which there are significant differences in event length are: april-march, may-march, november-march, july-april, august-april, september-april, july-may,august-may, spetember-may, october-may, july-june, september-june, september-july, november-july, september-august, november-august, october-september, november-september, december-september, november-october. Seems like september is consistently significantly different from the event lengths in other months?
# There is a significant difference in event length between: Evergreen Needleleaf Forests-Closed Shrublands(*), Evergreen Broadleaf Forests-Croplands(*), Evergreen Needleleaf Forests-Croplands(*), Grasslands-Croplands(*), Grasslands(*)-Evergreen Needleleaf Forests, Open Shrublands(*)-Evergreen Needleleaf Forests, Permanent Wetlands(*)-Evergreen Needleleaf Forests, Savannas(*)-Evergreen Needleleaf Forests, Woody Savannas(*)-Evergreen Needleleaf Forests. (*) is next to the one that is higher. 

# Format as lm
eventlength_aov2 <- lm(data = event_length, event_dur ~ ig_month + lc_name)
summary(eventlength_aov2)
#The Multiple R-squared is 0.1053. The Adjusted R-squared is 0.1004. This means that these variables don't explain much of the variation, and more variables should be added to the model. 
```

# Central Question ANOVA

###What is the relationship between land cover type and fire growth rate?

##Response variables: max, mean and min daily growth per event
##Predictor variable: Land cover

#We felt an ANOVA was the mosst appropriate to address this question
because the response variables are continuous, the predictor is
categorical, and individual fire events can be used as observational
units.

```{r - data setup, ANOVA}
#Load dplyr and make it so that there is only one row per fire event
library(dplyr)
fire_events <- california_events_processed |>
  distinct(id, .keep_all = TRUE)
#Make anova models for each with land cover type as the predictor variable
max_model <- aov(mx_grw_km2 ~ lc_name, data = fire_events)
min_model <- aov(mn_grw_km2 ~ lc_name, data = fire_events)
mean_model <- aov(mu_grw_km2 ~ lc_name, data = fire_events)

anova_summary <- data.frame(Metric = c("Maximum", "Mean", "Minimum"),
  F_value = c(summary(max_model)[[1]]["lc_name", "F value"],
    summary(mean_model)[[1]]["lc_name", "F value"],
    summary(min_model)[[1]]["lc_name", "F value"]),
  p_value = c(summary(max_model)[[1]]["lc_name", "Pr(>F)"],
    summary(mean_model)[[1]]["lc_name", "Pr(>F)"],
    summary(min_model)[[1]]["lc_name", "Pr(>F)"]))
anova_summary 
#plot residuals vs. fitted values for the mean model as a diagnostic
plot(mean_model, which = 1)
#plot Q-Q plot as a diagnostic
plot(mean_model, which = 2)
#Both the Q-Q and the residual plots raise red flags. Maybe a log transform will help?
mean_model_log <- aov(log1p(mu_grw_km2) ~ lc_name, data = fire_events)
#Diagnostic test again
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(mean_model_log, which = 1)
plot(mean_model_log, which = 2)
#Red flags are still there with the log transforms

#Since Pr(>F)<.001 for each anova model, we will run a post hoc Tukey test to interpret this statistical difference
TukeyHSD(max_model)
TukeyHSD(mean_model)
TukeyHSD(min_model)
#Sorting the Tukey tests so they are more readable
mean_sig <- as.data.frame(TukeyHSD(mean_model)$lc_name) |>
  filter(`p adj` < 0.05) |>
  arrange(`p adj`)

min_sig <- as.data.frame(TukeyHSD(max_model)$lc_name) |>
  filter(`p adj` < 0.05) |>
  arrange(`p adj`)

max_sig <- as.data.frame(TukeyHSD(min_model)$lc_name) |>
  filter(`p adj` < 0.05) |>
  arrange(`p adj`)

tukey_summary <- data.frame(Metric = c("Maximum", "Mean", "Minimum"),
  Significant_comparisons = c(nrow(max_sig), nrow(mean_sig), nrow(min_sig)))
tukey_summary
```

#The most strongly recurring pattern is open shrubland's significantly
high fire growth as compared to other land cover types.They have a
significantly higher mean daily growth than Croplands, Barren, and
Grasslands, a higher maximum daily growth than Croplands, Evergreen
Needleleaf Forests, and Barren, and higher minimums than Croplands,
Evergreen Needleleaf Forests, and Barren. Closed shrublands and
evergreen needleleef forests also have relatively high mean and maximum
daily growth levels, but not minimum indicating that they might have
relatively high growth during active periods but not throughout event
duration.

```{r - graphics}
#Load tidyr
library(tidyr)

#make dataframe with mean, sd for each of the three categories and pivot it 
growth_summary <- fire_events |>
  group_by(lc_name) |>
  summarize(
     max_growth = mean(mx_grw_km2, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_growth = mean(mu_grw_km2, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_growth = mean(mn_grw_km2, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_se = sd(mx_grw_km2, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(mx_grw_km2))),
    mean_se = sd(mu_grw_km2, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(mu_grw_km2))),
    min_se = sd(mn_grw_km2, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(mn_grw_km2))),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
se_long <- growth_summary |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(max_se, mean_se, min_se),names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "se")|>
  mutate(metric = recode(metric,max_se = "max_growth",mean_se = "mean_growth",
      min_se = "min_growth"))
growth_long <- growth_summary |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(max_growth, mean_growth, min_growth),names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "growth")
growth_long <- growth_long |>
  left_join(se_long, by = c("lc_name", "metric"))

#Make graphic plotting max/mean/min fire growth rates across land cover types
ggplot(growth_long, aes(x = growth, y = lc_name))+
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = growth - 1.96 * se, xmax = growth + 1.96 * se), width = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Daily fire growth (km²/day)",y = "Land cover type",
       title = "Daily fire growth across land cover types")

```
#This graphic plots daily fire growth on the X axis and land cover type per event on the X axis. As mentioned before, open shrubland's relatively high growth levels jumps out, especially given its significance after running the anova and tukey tests. Closed shrubland and evergreen needleleaf forests also have relatively high means. Some land cover types not mentioned earlier, like evergreen broadleaf forests and urban/built up lands also visually jump out as having possibly higher growth rates, but they were not found to be statistically significant after the Tukey tests, which is visible given the extremely high spread for both units.That represents one limitation of this figure - we felt it was important to include results for all of the land cover types so that the reader could parse all the data, but not all of them were statistically significant. The primary takeaway from this figure and the associated tables up above is to possibly take a deeper dive into open shrubland fire growth specifically, perhaps running some of the above tests filtered to examine only open shrubland. Examining needleleaf forests might provide useful results as well given their prevalence in California.
